newsitem.title: USA: AT&T Internet access chief forms new venture.
newsitem.headline: AT&T Internet access chief forms new venture.

text.p: AT&T Corp said Tom Evslin, chief of its WorldNet Internet access service, had resigned to run ITXC Corp, a new company that provides long-distance services to Internet-based phone service providers.

In a joint statement with VocalTec Communications Ltd, a Northvale, N.J.-based pioneer in Internet telephony software, AT&T and VocalTec said the two companies had signed unspecified agreements with ITXC.
In addition, they said that both AT&T and VocalTec will retain the option of taking equity stakes in ITXC.

The companies said Evslin, who is the founder of ITXC, would join the VocalTec board and both AT&T and VocalTec will have a seat on the ITXC board. VocalTec will provide ITXC with technology and software products.
ITXC, stands for "Internet telephony exchange carrier" a reference to the company's hybrid strategy of combining Internet telephony with interexchange, or long-distance phone services.
At AT&T, Evslin had served as vice president in charge of WorldNet Service since its inception last year.
The Internet access service had about 923,000 subscribers at the end of June, the company said.
Evslin will remain in charge of WorldNet until a successor is named.
ITXC plans to provide Internet phone service providers routing and settlement services, similar to those that already exist in the traditional phone industry.

The departure of a top-level AT&T executive to form an Internet phone start-up suggests that the emerging technology has rounded a corner and is gaining acceptance within the mainstream phone industry.
"The founding of ITXC is a watershed event in the ongoing convergence of the Internet, telephony, and computing markets," said Elon Ganor, the chief executive of VocalTec.

"ITXC will provide services for (Internet Telephone Service Providers) that are crucial to the development of a unified multimedia communications network spanning the public, switched telephone network and the Internet," he said.

While Evslin's move does not necessarily mean an end to his ties with AT&T, he joins an exodus of executives from AT&T over the last year that has highlighted the phone giant's predicament over attracting and keeping top-level managers.

"This illustrates that for those who have an entrepreneurial itch, you can't scratch it at AT&T," said Jeffrey Kagan, an industry analyst who runs Kagan Telecom Associates in Atlanta, in reaction to Evslin's move.
This is not a negative reflection on AT&T, but it suggests the problem the company faces retaining executive talent, he added.

Last week, John Walter, AT&T's president and chief operating officer, resigned after the company's board declined to elevate him to become chief executive according to a timetable originally laid out when he was hired in October.

Other top executives to depart in the last year include former president Alex Mandl, who left to take the top job at Teligent Inc., a wireless communications company, and Joe Nacchio, former head of consumer long distance at AT&T, who joined Qwest Communications International Inc a fiber-optic network service company.
